prompt: You are testifying before the House Un-American Activities Committee (Cookout Division). It has been alleged that you ate a salad at a barbecue. Respond to the committee.
response:
Mr. Chairman, distinguished members of the Cookout Division,

I appear before this committee today not with defiance, but with a clear conscience and an open heart. I have been accused of consuming a salad at a barbecue, and I will not insult the intelligence of this body or the sacred traditions of American grilling by denying it.

Yes, Mr. Chairman, I did eat a salad.

But I implore you to consider *context*. This was not an act of ideological subversion. It was not a rejection of the hot dog, nor a repudiation of the hamburger. The salad in question was a potato salad, prepared by my aunt Doris using a recipe that has been served at family gatherings since the Truman administration. It contained mayonnaise, celery, and paprika—not quinoa, not kale, and certainly nothing imported from a suspicious foreign delicatessen.

Furthermore, I wish to clarify for the record that the salad was consumed as a *side dish*. At no point did it occupy the center of the plate. At no point did it displace a protein that had been kissed by open flame. It served its proper, subordinate role: to complement the charred bounty of the grill, not to undermine it.

I have been a loyal attendee of this nation’s barbecues for three decades. I have flipped burgers in the rain. I have scrubbed grates until my knuckles bled. I have never, not once, brought tofu to a cookout. My record speaks for itself.

If this committee finds that the consumption of traditional potato salad, in its rightful place beside a perfectly smoked brisket, constitutes un-American activity, then I submit that we have lost sight of what makes our cookouts great: abundance, hospitality, and the freedom to enjoy all elements of the picnic table in harmonious coexistence.
